newsitem.title: UK: Eurobonds slow pre-weekend, quiet week in prospect.
newsitem.headline: Eurobonds slow pre-weekend, quiet week in prospect.

text.p: 1100 GMT - Primary market activity slowed ahead of the weekend, with just a handful of retail-targeted offerings emerging on Friday.
** Welcome Break's asset-backed sterling deal firmed up.
** Greece mandated Goldman Sachs and Nomura to lead manage two 50 billion yen Eurobonds next week, at 10 and 20 years.
** U.S. agency Federal Home Loan Board set a structured $200 million three-year deal, with call options on the semi-annual coupon dates after the first year.
** The Development Bank of Southern Africa set a zero coupon 5.0 billion rand 30-year deal.
New issue business was at a low ebb on Friday ahead of the weekend and just a handful of retail-targeted transactions were launched.
Next week promises to be fairly light, with U.S. jobs data for July due and the holiday month of August looming, dealers said.
One possible sizeable transaction will be the 321 million stg asset-backed deal being planned by Bahrain-based INVESTCORP's Welcome Break, a chain of motorway service stations in Britain.

There will be two fixed-rate tranches with maturities of about 18 years, worth 140 million stg, and 20 years (67 million stg) with the balance in 10-year (42 million stg) and 13-year (72 million stg) FRNs.
All tranches, which will amortise at varying rates, have been been provisionally rated A by S&P, except the 20-year leg which will be rated BBB.
The bonds will be backed by cash flows from Welcome Break's operations. Proceeds will repay loans taken out when INVESTCORP paid Granada Group 476 million stg for Welcome Break in February.
Bankers Trust and Chase Manhattan will be joint lead manager, with BZW a co-lead manager.
Sources close to the offering said the pricing will be "relatively generous", the Financial Times newspaper said on Friday.
The FT quoted a firm involved in the deal as saying: "This won't be priced as widely as a high-yield issue, but on the other hand it will offer a wider spread than on standard A-rated deals".
One definite sizeable transaction next week will be from Greece which mandated Goldman Sachs and Nomura to lead manage two 50 billion yen Eurobonds, with 10 and 20-year maturities.
Syndicate managers expected widespread distribution to investors in Japan, Germany, France, Britain and offshore U.S. funds.

Greece, rated Baa1 by Moody's Investors Service and BBB- by S&P, raised a total of 130 billion yen through the samurai market in three tranches via Nomura in July 1996. The bonds had six-, 12- and 20-year maturities.
